planting.note: Set container-grown vines in spring against a mailbox post, fence, or trellis in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Flava opens its earliest flowers in winter mild spells, well ahead of the typical Carolina jessamine bloom window.

directions: Flava is a named selection of Carolina jessamine grown for trumpet-shaped, golden-yellow flowers that begin opening during warm spells in winter and continue through the usual early-spring bloom flush. Give it well-drained soil and a permanent trellis, arbor, or fence to twine on, since like other Carolina jessamine it climbs by twining stems rather than clinging tendrils. Established plants tolerate heat, drought, and light shade, though full sun produces the heaviest flowering. Remember that all plant parts are toxic if ingested, and site it away from areas where children or pets graze on foliage.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring against masonry, a chain-link fence, or a heavy arbor where the adhesive tendril discs can grip; Wabash Valley was selected for reliable winter survival well north of the species' typical range, so it also performs dependably through Gulf Coast winters.

directions: Wabash Valley traces to a wild plant found by Dr. Wesley Whiteside near the Wabash River in southern Illinois, near the northern edge of crossvine's native range, and was introduced to the nursery trade for its unusually dependable cold hardiness. Its two-inch trumpet flowers are maroon-red outside and yellow-throated inside, appearing in flushes from mid-spring into early summer and drawing hummingbirds. Grow it on a sturdy permanent support since the tendrils cling directly to hard surfaces without needing to be tied or trained. Once established it tolerates heat, drought, and partial shade with only an occasional post-bloom trim to control size.

planting.note: Set container plants in spring against a trellis, arbor, or fence in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; give the self-clinging tendrils a rough surface to grip since this selection climbs as vigorously as typical crossvine.

directions: Yellow crossvine is a named selection valued for flowers that lack the reddish-orange exterior tones of typical crossvine, opening instead in soft, clear yellow with a slightly deeper yellow throat. It blooms heaviest in mid to late spring and draws hummingbirds and bees, then carries semi-evergreen foliage that can pick up bronze tones in cold winters. Give it a sturdy permanent structure since the vine is a vigorous, fast-growing climber capable of covering a large arbor or fence within a few seasons. Prune after the main spring bloom flush to control size and remove any wayward growth.

planting.note: Plant on a heavy-duty arbor, pergola, or pillar in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; like other American wisteria selections, Alba is far less rampant than Chinese or Japanese wisteria but still needs a permanent, sturdy support.

directions: Alba is a white-flowered selection of American wisteria, bearing mildly fragrant, pure white racemes in late spring that stand out against the vine's compound green foliage. It blooms on new growth rather than old wood, so a hard renewal prune in late winter will not sacrifice the coming season's flowers the way it would on Asian wisteria. Give it full sun for the heaviest bloom, though it tolerates light shade with some reduction in flowering. Established vines handle heat and short dry spells well but perform best with consistent moisture during their first two seasons.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Swantly Purple American Wisteria (Deep Purple-Violet Native Wisteria)

planting.note: Plant on a heavy-duty arbor, pergola, or pillar in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; this selection's deeper flower color is easiest to appreciate on a support that lets the racemes hang free where they can be viewed from below.

directions: Swantly Purple is a named American wisteria selection prized for fragrant racemes in a deeper, more intense purple-violet than the lavender tones typical of the species. Flowering occurs on new growth in late spring, with occasional light rebloom later in the season on well-established vines. Because it is far less aggressive than Chinese or Japanese wisteria, it can be grown on a normal residential arbor or pergola without the risk of the structure eventually being crushed. Prune immediately after the spring flush to shape the vine and keep it within bounds on its support.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
